summary: Sirach 3 begins with instruction to children about honoring father and mother, including care for a father in old age and warnings against dishonoring parents. The chapter then turns to humility, restraint before matters beyond one’s strength, the danger of pride and stubbornness, and the value of almsgiving and repaying good turns.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows Sirach’s wisdom as household instruction joined to teachability before God. It also introduces a pattern common in the book: ordinary conduct, such as family care, humility, and generosity, is treated as part of a wise life.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; the Greek translation was made later by his unnamed grandson.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal learning, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean culture in the background.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction using direct address, maxims, paired lines, vivid comparisons, and practical moral teaching.

outline.heading: Listen to parental instruction
outline.note: The speaker calls children to hear and do, grounding the command in the Lord’s honor for father and mother.

outline.heading: Honor father and mother
outline.note: Honoring parents is linked with atonement, treasure, joy, prayer, blessing, and family stability; dishonor brings shame rather than glory.

outline.heading: Care for an aging father
outline.note: The son is told to help, show patience, and avoid grief or dishonor; forsaking father and provoking mother are sharply condemned.

outline.heading: Humility before the Lord
outline.note: The student is urged to conduct business humbly; greatness is to be met with deeper humility, and the Lord is glorified by the lowly. Verse 19 is blank in the World English Bible.

outline.heading: Limits of human searching
outline.note: The reader is warned not to seek matters too hard or secret, because conceit and evil opinion can lead judgment astray.

outline.heading: Stubbornness, pride, and teachability
outline.note: A stubborn heart and pride lead to trouble, while the prudent heart understands a proverb and the wise person desires a listener’s ear.

outline.heading: Generosity and repayment
outline.note: Almsgiving is compared to water quenching fire, and the one who repays good turns is said to find support when falling.

keyVerses.text: Honor your father in deed and word, that a blessing may come upon you from him.
keyVerses.why: This sentence states the chapter’s first main duty in plain terms: honor is shown through both action and speech.

keyVerses.text: If he fails in understanding, have patience with him. Don’t dishonor him in your full strength.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the passage about caring for an aging father, especially when the child has strength and the parent has weakness.

keyVerses.text: The greater you are, humble yourself the more, and you will find favor before the Lord.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the chapter’s turn from family honor to humility before the Lord.

keyVerses.text: Water will quench a flaming fire; almsgiving will make atonement for sins.
keyVerses.why: This compact comparison introduces the closing emphasis on generosity and its stated effect in the chapter.

questions.question: Who is speaking at the start of the chapter?
questions.answer: The speaker identifies himself as “your father” and addresses “my children.” In the book’s wisdom-instruction setting, this sounds like a teacher using family language for students, though the chapter also speaks directly about actual fathers and mothers.

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by honoring father and mother?
questions.answer: The chapter describes honor as something done “in deed and word,” not only as a feeling. It includes listening, serving under parents, not glorifying oneself in a father’s dishonor, and helping a father in old age.

questions.question: What is meant by “atonement for sins” here?
questions.answer: The chapter says that honoring one’s father, kindness to one’s father, and almsgiving are connected with atonement for sins. It does not explain the mechanism in this chapter, so it is safest to say that Sirach presents these acts as having serious religious value before God rather than as merely social politeness.

questions.question: Does this chapter treat old age and failing understanding directly?
questions.answer: Yes. Verse 12 tells the son to help his father in old age, and verse 13 tells him to have patience if his father “fails in understanding.” The point in the chapter is not that weakness removes dignity, but that the stronger child must not dishonor the weakened parent.

questions.question: What does “humility” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: The word appears as a way of going about one’s business and as the proper response to increased greatness. The chapter connects humility with being loved, finding favor before the Lord, and being among the “lowly” through whom the Lord is glorified.

questions.question: Why is verse 19 blank in this edition?
questions.answer: The World English Bible leaves verse 19 blank. Sirach survives in different textual forms, and editions can differ in wording and verse numbering. Other editions may include additional lines or number the passage differently.

questions.question: Is the warning against seeking “things that are too hard” anti-learning?
questions.answer: The chapter itself does not reject learning; it praises knowledge, prudence, proverbs, and the ear of a listener. The warning is against overreaching into secret or beyond-strength matters in a way connected with conceit and slipped judgment. Readers differ on how broadly to apply that warning, but within the chapter it favors humble teachability over proud speculation.

questions.question: What is a “stubborn heart” in this chapter?
questions.answer: A stubborn heart is described by its outcome: it does badly, becomes burdened with troubles, and is paired with loving danger and heaping sin upon sins. The chapter contrasts it with the prudent heart that can understand a proverb.

questions.question: How does the chapter end?
questions.answer: It ends with two images of support. Almsgiving is compared to water putting out fire, and the person who repays good turns is said to find support “in the time of his falling.”

glossary.def: The chapter connects honoring one’s father and almsgiving with atonement for sins, without explaining how these actions bring it about.
The stage in which the son is told to help his father and not grieve him as long as he lives.
The posture the student is told to bring to business and to greatness before the Lord.
Matters the chapter says the reader does not need, in contrast to “the things that have been commanded you.”
